posts.content:
My book is out today: The Work That Remains — Human Judgment, AI, and the Architecture of the Next Enterprise.

I wrote it because most of what executives hear about AI comes from one of two rooms — one in panic, one in euphoria. Neither helps you decide anything. What enterprises need is a pragmatic account of where AI is genuinely strong, where it is structurally limited, and a deployment model that follows from both. That is what this book tries to be.

My bias, declared up front: I run an automation company, and the conclusion is convenient for companies like mine. Do not take the argument on my authority — and do not dismiss it for the same reason.

If you leave with one argument, take this one. AI genuinely embodies characteristics of human intelligence — it reasons, plans, drafts, explains. But it lacks the one thing every employee you ever hired does naturally: it does not learn on the job. A new hire arrives knowing nothing about your company and becomes valuable by absorbing everything nobody ever wrote down. The model arrives brilliant — and shows up exactly as new every morning. The entire method in this book is built around that limitation.

I wrote it with Claude and ChatGPT, and the last chapter explains how. I learned more about AI writing this book than in any year of running an AI company. I think every reader will leave with something that changes how they deploy it.

Read it here: https://lnkd.in/g3PwkM4q

posts.content:
It turns out 30 minutes isn’t enough time when someone lets me talk about innovation. 😄

I had a great time joining CEO of Silicon Valley Executive Academy, Victoria Mensch for Decisions at the Frontier.

Some of my biggest reflections went back to the concept of “innovator’s dimemma”. Yes, still relevant...

• Every successful company eventually needs an Act Two.
• At UiPath, our Act Two is the shift from leading in RPA to helping shape the future of agentic automation.
• But an Act Two pivot doesn’t mean abandoning what worked. It means building on the strengths of Act One and applying them to what comes next.

See the change early. Act before all the data is obvious. Build from strength.

You can’t wait for the market to tell you it’s time to reinvent.

posts.content:
Testing is often completed, but not properly preserved.

When documentation is scattered across spreadsheets, screenshots and emails, it becomes difficult to establish what was tested, which version was used and who approved the results.

This creates avoidable risks during audits, system upgrades and knowledge transfers.

For leaders, the key question is not only how efficiently testing is executed, but whether quality evidence remains reliable, traceable and usable over time.

How confident are you that your testing documentation would withstand your next audit or major system change?
